claims.text: A high-entropy alloy contains at least five elements, each at no less than 5 atomic percent.
The starting alloy is a near-equiatomic, disordered solid solution.
Increasing variance in constituent atomic radii increases local lattice distortion in a random HEA solid solution.
Greater local lattice distortion weakens the uniformity of electron-phonon coupling.
Greater local lattice distortion lowers the density of states at the Fermi level.
Weaker or less uniform electron-phonon coupling and a lower Fermi-level density of states reduce the superconducting transition temperature.
An HEA optimized to minimize atomic-size mismatch should have a higher transition temperature than an otherwise controlled HEA with greater mismatch.
An HEA optimized to minimize atomic-size mismatch should exhibit a more spatially uniform superconducting gap.
The alloy with larger atomic-size mismatch will show a lower transition temperature than the low-mismatch baseline.
The alloy with larger atomic-size mismatch will show greater spatial variation in its superconducting gap than the low-mismatch baseline.
Atomic-size mismatch can be varied between two alloys while their overall composition remains identical.
The effect of atomic-size mismatch can be isolated while overall electronic concentration and phase structure remain fixed.
Near-ambient pressure and an inert atmosphere will maintain phase stability during cryogenic measurements.
The proposed mechanism applies to single-phase random-solid-solution HEAs but not to cases in which mismatch induces secondary phases.
Bonding changes and unforeseen phase evolution may confound the relationship between size mismatch and superconductivity.
Local structural disorder can be relevant to superconducting properties in disordered superconductors.

contradictions.description: The intervention says to alter elemental makeup to change atomic-size variance, while the predicted comparison and experiment require identical overall compositions. For fixed element identities and atomic fractions, atomic-size variance is fixed, so these controls cannot realize the stated intervention without an additional mechanism such as changing ordering, strain, or isotope identity.

The initial state is only a generic near-equiatomic HEA, whereas the stated baseline is a separately engineered minimum-size-variance alloy. It is therefore unclear whether the baseline is the starting material requested for the controlled comparison.
